items: Measure your cat's claw width to select the correct cap size, not based on cat size — if the cap covers more than two-thirds of the visible claw, go up a size immediately.
If caps fall off immediately or bunch at the tip, adjust the size accordingly — an improperly sized cap causes discomfort that makes your cat pull it off.
Use only the adhesive that comes packaged with the caps — substitute glues do not bond properly and cause caps to fall off within days.
Clean each claw with a damp cotton ball before applying caps — the adhesive bonds to clean keratin, not to the oils and debris on unwashed claws.
Gently press the paw pad to extend the claws fully before sliding each cap on — holding the cap in place for 5 full seconds ensures the adhesive cures properly.

Start with the front paws only and limit sessions to two paws per day if your cat resists handling — forcing all four paws at once creates negative associations that make future applications impossible.
Set a recurring 4-week calendar reminder to replace all caps — caps shed off naturally with the outer claw sheath, and one missed cycle means weeks of fully exposed claws.
Size down immediately if your cat removes caps within days of application — the discomfort of a too-large cap is the primary reason most cats persistently pull them off.
Switch to claw filing if caps consistently fail despite correct sizing and adhesive — use a human emery board or cat-specific nail file instead of clippers, which can split large claws.
File claws every 7 to 10 days, focusing on the front paws — rounding the sharp tip removes damage-causing edges without reshaping the claw structure.
Round each claw tip until it no longer catches on drywall or fabric when tested — the goal is dulling the point, not changing the claw's natural shape.
Add enrichment activities if your cat pulls caps off as a stress response — address the anxiety driving displacement behavior rather than expecting caps alone to solve scratching issues.
